requirements.requirement: Verify that input is decoded or unescaped into a canonical form only once, it is only decoded when encoded data in that form is expected, and that this is done before processing the input further, for example it is not performed after input validation or sanitization.
requirements.rationale: Decoding happens once, at the framework boundary, before any validation runs. Werkzeug percent-decodes the path and form values as it parses the request; nothing in the application decodes again, and a search of the package finds no unquote call on request data - the one unquote in the codebase is in the log scrubber, applied to a Referer header for redaction rather than for processing. Validation therefore always sees the canonical form, never a re-decoded one.
requirements.verification: Grep the package for unquote/urldecode/base64 applied to request data; confirm each validator runs on the value Werkzeug produced; submit a double-encoded traversal sequence and confirm it is treated as literal text.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application performs output encoding and escaping either as a final step before being used by the interpreter for which it is intended or by the interpreter itself.
requirements.rationale: Encoding is the interpreter's own, applied as it renders. Jinja2 autoescapes at output time for HTML; SQLAlchemy binds parameters so the database receives value and statement separately; flask.jsonify serialises through json.dumps; url_for percent-encodes each parameter for its position. There is no place where a value is escaped early and then carried through further processing, which is the failure mode this requirement describes.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_jinja_templates_compile_with_autoescape and TestInjectionSurfaces; confirm no view pre-escapes a value before passing it to a template.

requirements.requirement: Verify that output encoding for an HTTP response, HTML document, or XML document is relevant for the context required, such as encoding the relevant characters for HTML elements, HTML attributes, HTML comments, CSS, or HTTP header fields, to avoid changing the message or document structure.
requirements.rationale: Every HTML response is rendered by Jinja2 with autoescape on, and a test walks the AST of every template in the loader to assert that no template disables it and none applies the `safe` filter. Values reach HTML element and attribute contexts only; the application builds no CSS or XML documents and writes no user data into a response header field. Header values that are set are fixed strings from security/headers.py.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_jinja_templates_compile_with_autoescape, which parses and compiles every registered template; add a template with `|safe` and confirm it fails.

requirements.requirement: Verify that when dynamically building URLs, untrusted data is encoded according to its context (e.g., URL encoding or base64url encoding for query or path parameters). Ensure that only safe URL protocols are permitted (e.g., disallow javascript: or data:).
requirements.rationale: URLs are built with Flask's url_for, which percent-encodes every parameter for its position in the path or query. The one place a user-supplied URL is emitted as an href is a DocLink, and validation.URL_SCHEMES is an allowlist of exactly {http, https} - javascript:, data:, vbscript: and file: are refused because they are not on it rather than because they were predicted. Share codes are emitted in a fragment and are generated, not supplied.
requirements.verification: Re-run TestBrowserFacingControls; inspect validation.URL_SCHEMES and the DocLink form validator; grep the templates for an href built by string concatenation rather than url_for.

JSON responses are produced by flask.jsonify, which serialises through json.dumps and sets application/json; no response body is assembled by string formatting.

requirements.requirement: Verify that data selection or database queries (e.g., SQL, HQL, NoSQL, Cypher) use parameterized queries, ORMs, entity frameworks, or are otherwise protected from SQL Injection and other database injection attacks. This is also relevant when writing stored procedures.

There are no stored procedures.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application sanitizes or disables user-supplied scriptable or expression template language content, such as Markdown, CSS or XSL stylesheets, BBCode, or similar.
requirements.rationale: Markdown is accepted as an upload but is never rendered: a .md file is stored as bytes and served as an attachment with a sandbox CSP and nosniff, exactly like a PDF, so its scriptable constructs are never interpreted by anything. No CSS, XSL, BBCode or template content is accepted from a user in any field. Templates themselves are files on disk and are never built from input - see 1.3.7.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application protects against Server-side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks, by validating untrusted data against an allowlist of protocols, domains, paths and ports and sanitizing potentially dangerous characters before using the data to call another service.
requirements.rationale: Two layers, and the outer one is now the load-bearing part. At the application layer the lookup pins the scheme, host and path from a dict in code, refuses redirects, and validates resolved addresses against private ranges - but the DNS name is resolved once for validation and again by the transport when connecting, so a rebinding attack between the two remains open and is not closed by this review. What has changed is the layer beneath: the application container no longer has any route off the host, so a successful SSRF reaches nothing. The feature is also off unless an operator sets BARCODE_LOOKUP_PROVIDER, which requires adding the edge network back and is therefore a reviewable change rather than a default. Recorded as a finding; the rebinding defect is real and unfixed.
requirements.verification: Pin validated addresses in the transport with correct TLS hostname verification, then add regression tests for a changing DNS answer, IPv6 and redirect behaviour. Until then, confirm docker-compose keeps `web` off the edge network and BARCODE_LOOKUP_PROVIDER unset.

Every f-string and .format call in the package has a literal template with user data as an argument, which is the safe direction; the pattern this requirement warns about - a user-supplied template applied to application data - does not occur. requirements.requirement: Verify that the application uses memory-safe string, safer memory copy and pointer arithmetic to detect or prevent stack, buffer, or heap overflows.
requirements.rationale: The application is Python, which has no pointer arithmetic, bounds-checks every sequence access and manages string memory itself; a stack, buffer or heap overflow is not expressible in the code under review. The memory-unsafe surface is confined to the C extensions the runtime image ships - Pillow, libmagic, psycopg, argon2-cffi and CPython itself - and that surface is managed the way it has to be, by keeping them current: Renovate proposes updates continuously and two image scanners gate every build on the versions actually present.

requirements.requirement: Verify that sign, range, and input validation techniques are used to prevent integer overflows.
requirements.rationale: Python integers are arbitrary precision, so an application-level integer overflow is not possible. Where a value has to fit a database type it is range-validated before it gets there: quantity is bounded between QUANTITY_MIN and QUANTITY_MAX by a WTForms NumberRange, the column type and a Postgres CHECK, and depth is bounded the same way. Sign is checked rather than assumed - a negative quantity is refused by all three layers rather than wrapping.

requirements.rationale: Memory is reclaimed by the interpreter; there are no pointers to dangle and no frees to get wrong. The resources that do need explicit release are files, database sessions and image handles, and each is released deterministically: image decoding uses a with block, the scoped session is removed at application-context teardown, and uploaded blobs are deleted only after a query confirms no other attachment row references the same bytes - the case that would otherwise pull data out from under a live row.

requirements.requirement: Verify that transactions are being used at the business logic level such that either a business logic operation succeeds in its entirety or it is rolled back to the previous correct state.
requirements.rationale: Every mutating request runs inside one SQLAlchemy transaction that is committed at the end or rolled back by the application-context teardown, so a failure part-way leaves no partial state. The audit row is written in the same transaction as the change it records, which is what makes the ledger match reality rather than merely accompany it; the one deliberate exception is a denial audit, which commits immediately because the request that follows it aborts and would otherwise discard the row. A refused form writes nothing at all, which a test demonstrates.

requirements.requirement: Verify that business logic level locking mechanisms are used to ensure that limited quantity resources (such as theater seats or delivery slots) cannot be double-booked by manipulating the application's logic.
requirements.rationale: Two locks, for the two places a limited resource exists. A checkout takes the item row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE through get_owned_for_update, so two concurrent attempts to take custody of the same item serialise and the second sees the first's result. The audit chain takes a transaction-scoped advisory lock before computing the next sequence number, so two concurrent writers cannot read the same head and fork the chain. Quantity changes are computed by the database from the current value rather than submitted by the client, so a lost update is not expressible.
requirements.verification: Re-run tests/test_custody.py and tests/test_audit_chain.py; run two concurrent checkouts of one item and confirm one fails.

requirements.requirement: Verify that each cookie's 'SameSite' attribute value is set according to the purpose of the cookie, to limit exposure to user interface redress attacks and browser-based request forgery attacks, commonly known as cross-site request forgery (CSRF).
requirements.rationale: SameSite=Lax on the session cookie, which is the value the purpose calls for: the application is navigated to from printed labels and external links, so Strict would drop the session on arrival and present a signed-in user with a sign-in page, while Lax still withholds the cookie from every cross-site POST - the shape CSRF takes. It is one of three layers, alongside CSRF tokens and the strict Referer check, rather than the only one.
requirements.verification: Inspect SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE in config.py and the Set-Cookie on a live response; issue a cross-site POST and confirm the cookie is absent.

requirements.requirement: Verify that cookies have the '__Host-' prefix for the cookie name unless they are explicitly designed to be shared with other hosts.
requirements.rationale: Production session cookie uses __Host- and is not shared with other hosts.
requirements.verification: Inspect the full quoted requirement against the referenced implementation and rerun the container suite; deployment-specific claims require the recorded proxy/role probes.

requirements.requirement: Verify that if the value of a cookie is not meant to be accessible to client-side scripts (such as a session token), the cookie must have the 'HttpOnly' attribute set and the same value (e. g. session token) must only be transferred to the client via the 'Set-Cookie' header field.
requirements.rationale: The session cookie is HttpOnly, and the token exists nowhere a script could read it even if it were not: it is written only in Set-Cookie, never rendered into a page, never placed in a URL, never put in localStorage or sessionStorage, and never returned in a response body. The __Host- prefix is on it as well, which is browser-enforced rather than advisory.
requirements.verification: Re-run tests/test_headers.py and tests/test_asvs_l1_gaps.py's cookie-prefix test; grep the templates and scripts for any reference to the session cookie name.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a Strict-Transport-Security header field is included on all responses to enforce an HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) policy. A maximum age of at least 1 year must be defined, and for L2 and up, the policy must apply to all subdomains as well.
requirements.rationale: max-age=31536000 (one year) with includeSubDomains, set by the application on every response and independently by the edge. The gap that made this Partial - a Caddy-generated 502 during a container replacement carrying no security headers at all - is closed: handle_errors now serves edge-generated responses with the full set, and the probe in evidence/proxy-edge-headers.txt records a 502, a proxied 200 and the plaintext redirect all carrying HSTS.
requirements.verification: Re-run the probe in evidence/proxy-edge-headers.txt against caddy/Caddyfile: stop the application container and confirm the 502 still carries HSTS with a one-year max-age and includeSubDomains.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) Access-Control-Allow-Origin header field is a fixed value by the application, or if the Origin HTTP request header field value is used, it is validated against an allowlist of trusted origins. When 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' needs to be used, verify that the response does not include any sensitive information.
requirements.rationale: The application emits no CORS headers under any circumstances: no CORS extension is installed, no view sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and no response reflects the Origin request header. Cross-origin reads are therefore refused by the browser's default same-origin policy, which is the most restrictive outcome the requirement admits, and there is no allowlist to get wrong.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_no_response_ever_grants_a_cross_origin_reader, which sends a hostile Origin to four endpoints and asserts no Access-Control-* header comes back.

requirements.requirement: Verify that HTTP responses include a Content-Security-Policy response header field which defines directives to ensure the browser only loads and executes trusted content or resources, in order to limit execution of malicious JavaScript. As a minimum, a global policy must be used which includes the directives object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none' and defines either an allowlist or uses nonces or hashes. For an L3 application, a per-response policy with nonces or hashes must be defined.
requirements.rationale: A global policy on every response, carrying object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none' as the requirement names, plus an allowlist: default-src, script-src, style-src, connect-src and form-action are all 'self'. The absence of unsafe-inline is what makes script-src 'self' hold without nonces - every script is an external file under /static and no template carries an inline handler, which the autoescape test enforces by parsing rather than by convention. Per-response nonces are an L3 obligation and are not claimed.
requirements.verification: Re-run tests/test_headers.py; inspect the header on a live response in evidence/proxy-headers.txt; add an inline script to a template and confirm the browser refuses to run it.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all HTTP responses contain an 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' header field. This instructs browsers not to use content sniffing and MIME type guessing for the given response, and to require the response's Content-Type header field value to match the destination resource. For example, the response to a request for a style is only accepted if the response's Content-Type is 'text/css'. This also enables the use of the Cross-Origin Read Blocking (CORB) functionality by the browser.
requirements.rationale: Set by the application on every response and again at the edge, including on the responses the application never produces. The gap that made this Partial - a Caddy-generated 502 during a container replacement carrying no security headers at all - is closed by the handle_errors route, and the probe in evidence/proxy-edge-headers.txt records nosniff on a proxied 200, a Caddy 502 and the plaintext redirect. Stored files carry it a third time, set explicitly in the download handler.
requirements.verification: Re-run the probe in evidence/proxy-edge-headers.txt with the application container stopped; re-run tests/test_headers.py.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application sets a referrer policy to prevent leakage of technically sensitive data to third-party services via the 'Referer' HTTP request header field. This can be done using the Referrer-Policy HTTP response header field or via HTML element attributes. Sensitive data could include path and query data in the URL, and for internal non-public applications also the hostname.
requirements.rationale: Referrer-Policy: same-origin on every response, which sends no referrer at all cross-origin and so cannot leak a path, a query or the internal hostname to a third party a user clicks through to. It is deliberately not no-referrer, which looks stricter and breaks Flask-WTF's strict Referer check on every HTTPS POST - two correct controls that cancel out, argued in D-22. Share pages set it a second time in their own after_request.
requirements.verification: Re-run tests/test_headers.py's referrer tests; follow an outbound documentation link from a share page and confirm no Referer is sent.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the web application uses the frame-ancestors directive of the Content-Security-Policy header field for every HTTP response to ensure that it cannot be embedded by default and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary. Note that the X-Frame-Options header field, although supported by browsers, is obsolete and may not be relied upon.
requirements.rationale: frame-ancestors 'none' in the CSP on every response, with X-Frame-Options: DENY alongside it for browsers that still read it - the requirement notes the latter is obsolete and must not be relied upon, and it is not: the CSP directive is the control. Edge-generated responses now carry the same directive, which is the gap that made this Partial.
requirements.verification: Re-run the probe in evidence/proxy-edge-headers.txt; attempt to frame the application and confirm the browser refuses.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the application does not rely on the CORS preflight mechanism to prevent disallowed cross-origin requests to use sensitive functionality, these requests are validated to ensure they originate from the application itself. This may be done by using and validating anti-forgery tokens or requiring extra HTTP header fields that are not CORS-safelisted request-header fields. This is to defend against browser-based request forgery attacks, commonly known as cross-site request forgery (CSRF).
requirements.rationale: The application does not rely on preflight. Every state-changing route is a POST carrying a Flask-WTF CSRF token bound to the session, WTF_CSRF_ENABLED is on outside the test configuration, WTF_CSRF_SSL_STRICT additionally checks the Referer on HTTPS, and the session cookie is SameSite=Lax so a cross-site POST arrives without it. The token is now signed with HMAC-SHA256 rather than the library default of HMAC-SHA1.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_a_post_without_a_csrf_token_is_refused, which builds an application with CSRF enabled rather than asserting the test configuration; confirm SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE and WTF_CSRF_SSL_STRICT in config.py.

This may require checking the values of the 'Origin' and 'Content-Type' request header fields or using an extra header field that is not a CORS-safelisted header-field.
requirements.rationale: CSRF defense uses Flask-WTF tokens, not CORS preflight.

requirements.requirement: Verify that HTTP requests to sensitive functionality use appropriate HTTP methods such as POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, and not methods defined by the HTTP specification as "safe" such as HEAD, OPTIONS, or GET. Alternatively, strict validation of the Sec-Fetch-* request header fields can be used to ensure that the request did not originate from an inappropriate cross-origin call, a navigation request, or a resource load (such as an image source) where this is not expected.
requirements.rationale: Every route that changes state is POST-only, including logout - a GET /logout can be fired by an tag on any page the user visits. A test enumerates the URL map and asserts that any path not served by a GET answers 405 to one, so a new mutating route that forgets the method restriction fails the suite rather than shipping.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_state_changing_endpoints_refuse_get and test_logout_and_delete_are_not_reachable_by_get; add a GET-able mutating route and confirm the suite fails.

requirements.requirement: Verify that separate applications are hosted on different hostnames to leverage the restrictions provided by same-origin policy, including how documents or scripts loaded by one origin can interact with resources from another origin and hostname-based restrictions on cookies.
requirements.rationale: There is one application on one hostname. Nothing else is hosted alongside it - the Caddy configuration defines a single site with a single reverse-proxy route and no other backend, and the uploads volume is deliberately not mounted at the edge - so there is no second application whose origin this one would need to be separated from. Applicability, not an unmet separation: the condition the requirement governs does not exist.
requirements.verification: Inspect caddy/Caddyfile for additional site blocks or routes. Re-assess if anything else is ever served from this hostname.

requirements.requirement: Verify that messages received by the postMessage interface are discarded if the origin of the message is not trusted, or if the syntax of the message is invalid.
requirements.rationale: No postMessage listener or cross-document messaging feature is present in the static JavaScript.
requirements.verification: Reinspect the named implementation against the full requirement; rerun relevant tests after any feature, protocol or deployment change.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application only uses client-side technologies which are still supported and considered secure. Examples of technologies which do not meet this requirement include NSAPI plugins, Flash, Shockwave, ActiveX, Silverlight, NACL, or client-side Java applets.
requirements.rationale: The client side is HTML, CSS and four files of plain ES5-compatible JavaScript. There is no plugin technology of any kind - no Flash, Shockwave, ActiveX, Silverlight, NACL or applet - and the CSP's object-src 'none' means none could be loaded even if a page tried. The two browser APIs used, getUserMedia for barcode scanning and Web NFC, are current standards rather than legacy extensions.
requirements.verification: Grep the templates for object, embed and applet elements; confirm object-src 'none' in the CSP; list the contents of static/js.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application will only automatically redirect the user to a different hostname or domain (which is not controlled by the application) where the destination appears on an allowlist.
requirements.rationale: There is no allowlist because there is no automatic redirect off-origin at all: is_safe_redirect refuses anything that is not a relative path beginning with a single slash - any scheme, any netloc, a protocol-relative //host, a backslash, whitespace or a control character - and every redirect in the application goes through it. The stricter position is also the simpler one; an allowlist would be a list of hosts to keep correct.
requirements.verification: Re-run tests/test_redirects.py and test_redirect_rejects_browser_normalization; submit an absolute URL as ?next= and confirm the fallback is used.

requirements.requirement: Verify that every HTTP response with a message body contains a Content-Type header field that matches the actual content of the response, including the charset parameter to specify safe character encoding (e.g., UTF-8, ISO-8859-1) according to IANA Media Types, such as "text/", "/+xml" and "/xml".
requirements.rationale: Flask sets Content-Type on every response with a body: text/html; charset=utf-8 for rendered templates, application/json for jsonify, and for stored files the type sniffed from the bytes at upload rather than guessed from a name. A test walks the main response-producing endpoints and asserts a Content-Type is present and carries a charset parameter wherever the type is text/*.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_every_body_carrying_response_declares_its_type; request a stored document and confirm the served type is the sniffed one.

requirements.requirement: Verify that only user-facing endpoints (intended for manual web-browser access) automatically redirect from HTTP to HTTPS, while other services or endpoints do not implement transparent redirects. This is to avoid a situation where a client is erroneously sending unencrypted HTTP requests, but since the requests are being automatically redirected to HTTPS, the leakage of sensitive data goes undiscovered.
requirements.rationale: The plaintext listener does exactly one thing - 308 to the HTTPS URL - and the application behind it is entirely user-facing: every route renders a page or serves a file to a browser. There is no machine-to-machine endpoint that a client could be silently redirecting to and no API surface whose caller would not notice. The one JSON response, the barcode lookup, is fetched by this application's own page from the same origin.
requirements.verification: Inspect the http:// site block in caddy/Caddyfile; confirm the route list contains no non-browser endpoint.

requirements.requirement: Verify that any HTTP header field used by the application and set by an intermediary layer, such as a load balancer, a web proxy, or a backend-for-frontend service, cannot be overridden by the end-user. Example headers might include X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-*, or X-User-ID.
requirements.rationale: Two halves of one control, and both are required. Caddy sets X-Forwarded-For to a value it chooses with header_up rather than appending to whatever arrived, so a client cannot seed the chain; ProxyFix is configured with x_for=1, which takes the last entry - the one Caddy wrote - rather than trusting more hops than exist. The value Caddy forwards is {client_ip}, which with no trusted_proxies declared - the shipped default - is the direct peer, so a forged header is ignored; declaring an operator's own upstream proxy trusted makes it resolve the real client out of that proxy's chain instead. Both behaviours are recorded in evidence/proxy-client-ip.txt. X-Forwarded-Port is trusted at zero hops because Caddy does not overwrite it, which was a finding in this review.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_a_client_cannot_forge_the_address_used_for_rate_limiting and test_untrusted_forwarded_port_cannot_override_proxy_host; send a forged X-Forwarded-For through the live edge and confirm the logged address is the peer's.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all application components (including load balancers, firewalls, and application servers) determine boundaries of incoming HTTP messages using the appropriate mechanism for the HTTP version to prevent HTTP request smuggling. In HTTP/1.x, if a Transfer-Encoding header field is present, the Content-Length header must be ignored per RFC 2616. When using HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, if a Content-Length header field is present, the receiver must ensure that it is consistent with the length of the DATA frames.
requirements.rationale: One HTTP implementation parses each version, and neither accepts an ambiguous framing. Caddy speaks HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 only - h3 is switched off in the global block - and Go's net/http rejects a request carrying both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length rather than choosing between them, which is the HTTP/1.x half of this requirement, and validates DATA frame lengths against any Content-Length for the HTTP/2 half. There is no second proxy in front of it to disagree with, which is the condition smuggling actually needs.
requirements.verification: Inspect the protocols directive in caddy/Caddyfile; send a request with conflicting Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length and confirm it is rejected rather than interpreted.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a query allowlist, depth limiting, amount limiting, or query cost analysis is used to prevent GraphQL or data layer expression Denial of Service (DoS) as a result of expensive, nested queries.
requirements.rationale: There is no GraphQL endpoint and no data-layer expression language exposed to a client. Every query is constructed server-side from a fixed set of views; a client supplies parameters, never a query, so there is no nesting depth or query cost for a caller to control. A test asserts no /graphql route is registered.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_no_documentation_or_introspection_endpoint_is_registered; confirm no GraphQL library is in the lockfile.

requirements.requirement: Verify that GraphQL introspection queries are disabled in the production environment unless the GraphQL API is meant to be used by other parties.
requirements.rationale: No GraphQL API exists, so there is no introspection to disable. Same evidence as 4.3.1.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_no_documentation_or_introspection_endpoint_is_registered.

requirements.requirement: Verify that WebSocket over TLS (WSS) is used for all WebSocket connections.
requirements.rationale: The application opens no WebSocket connections. There is no ws:// or wss:// URL in the source, no WebSocket library in requirements.in, and Caddy is configured with `protocols h1 h2` and no WebSocket upgrade route. Applicability, not absence of a control: there is no connection for the requirement to govern.

requirements.rationale: The application opens no WebSocket connections, so there is no handshake whose Origin could be checked. Same applicability as 4.4.1: no ws:// or wss:// URL in the source, no WebSocket library in the lockfile, and Caddy configured with h1 and h2 and no upgrade route.
requirements.verification: Grep the source and lockfile for websocket/socketio; inspect the Caddyfile for an upgrade handler. Re-assess if any real-time feature is added.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the application's standard session management cannot be used, dedicated tokens are being used for this, which comply with the relevant Session Management security requirements.
requirements.rationale: No WebSocket channel exists, and the standard session mechanism covers every request the application serves. There is no second channel needing tokens of its own.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the documentation defines the permitted file types, expected file extensions, and maximum size (including unpacked size) for each upload feature. Additionally, ensure that the documentation specifies how files are made safe for end-users to download and process, such as how the application behaves when a malicious file is detected.
requirements.rationale: POLICIES.md section 10 states the permitted types, the expected extension for each, the per-file size limit and where it is enforced, the decoded pixel ceiling, the per-request file count and the per-account ceilings - and, because the requirement asks for it explicitly, how a file is made safe for download and what happens when a malicious one is detected. That last paragraph names the gap rather than papering over it: there is no malware scanner, so a document that is malicious to its own owner's reader would be stored and served back unchanged, which is why 5.4.3 is Not met rather than compensated. Archives are not accepted, so there is no unpacked size to bound.
requirements.verification: Read POLICIES.md section 10 against validation.py's constants and security/uploads.py's pipeline; confirm each documented limit is the one enforced.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application will only accept files of a size which it can process without causing a loss of performance or a denial of service attack.
requirements.rationale: Four bounds, in the order the bytes arrive: Caddy refuses a body over 12 MB, Werkzeug refuses a declared Content-Length over MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH (10 MB) before buffering it, _read_bounded refuses an individual part over the same limit because one multipart body can carry several, and image decoding is refused above MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS before any pixel is decoded - a decompression bomb is a few kilobytes on the wire. Per-owner byte and file-count quotas bound the aggregate.
requirements.verification: Re-run tests/test_uploads.py and test_image_pixel_limit_is_a_hard_limit; post a 13 MB body and confirm it is refused before reaching Python.

requirements.requirement: Verify that when the application accepts a file, either on its own or within an archive such as a zip file, it checks if the file extension matches an expected file extension and validates that the contents correspond to the type represented by the extension. This includes, but is not limited to, checking the initial 'magic bytes', performing image re-writing, and using specialized libraries for file content validation. For L1, this can focus just on files which are used to make specific business or security decisions. For L2 and up, this must apply to all files being accepted.
requirements.rationale: Both halves are now present. Content is identified by libmagic from the bytes and checked against an allowlist; images are fully decoded and re-encoded into a new container, which destroys polyglots; and the submitted filename extension is checked against a per-type table so a JPEG named report.pdf is refused rather than silently stored under a corrected name. The stored name is still generated from the sniffed type and never derived from the submitted one.
requirements.verification: Re-run TestUploadExtensionMatchesContent, which covers a matching name, three mismatched ones, a missing extension, mixed case, and Markdown (which libmagic reports as text/plain).

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application checks compressed files (e.g., zip, gz, docx, odt) against maximum allowed uncompressed size and against maximum number of files before uncompressing the file.
requirements.rationale: No archive extraction feature; archive/document containers such as zip/docx are excluded by MIME allowlist.
requirements.verification: Reinspect the named implementation against the full requirement; rerun relevant tests after any feature, protocol or deployment change.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a file size quota and maximum number of files per user are enforced to ensure that a single user cannot fill up the storage with too many files, or excessively large files.
requirements.rationale: Both ceilings now exist and neither implies the other: 2 GB of bytes and 5,000 files per owner, checked together before anything is written. The file count is what closes the gap that made this Partial - five thousand one-kilobyte files sit well inside the byte quota and still cost an inode, a row and a directory entry each. A test exercises the count ceiling with the byte quota nowhere near exhausted.
requirements.verification: Re-run TestFileCountQuota; set MAX_ATTACHMENTS_PER_OWNER low and confirm the refusal happens inside the byte quota.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application rejects uploaded images with a pixel size larger than the maximum allowed, to prevent pixel flood attacks.
requirements.rationale: Explicit dimensions check now rejects images above the declared pixel ceiling before decoding, including the Pillow warning-only range.
requirements.verification: Inspect the full quoted requirement against the referenced implementation and rerun the container suite; deployment-specific claims require the recorded proxy/role probes.

requirements.requirement: Verify that files uploaded or generated by untrusted input and stored in a public folder, are not executed as server-side program code when accessed directly with an HTTP request.
requirements.rationale: Uploads are stored on a volume outside any web root and Caddy has no file_server directive for it, so there is no public folder for the question to arise in. The only path to a stored file is an authenticated handler that looks the row up under an ownership filter and serves it with a sandbox CSP, nosniff and an attachment disposition. Stored names are generated UUIDs with an extension derived from the sniffed type, and the runtime container executes nothing from that volume.
requirements.verification: Re-run TestBrowserFacingControls; inspect the Caddyfile for any file_server over the uploads volume; confirm docker-compose mounts the volume only into the application container.

requirements.requirement: Verify that when the application creates file paths for file operations, instead of user-submitted filenames, it uses internally generated or trusted data, or if user-submitted filenames or file metadata must be used, strict validation and sanitization must be applied. This is to protect against path traversal, local or remote file inclusion (LFI, RFI), and server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks.
requirements.rationale: Stored paths use generated names with containment checking; original filenames are display-only. Tests exercise traversal and upload authorization.
requirements.verification: Inspect the full quoted requirement against the referenced implementation and rerun the container suite; deployment-specific claims require the recorded proxy/role probes.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application validates or ignores user-submitted filenames, including in a JSON, JSONP, or URL parameter and specifies a filename in the Content-Disposition header field in the response.
requirements.rationale: Original filenames are stripped of control/separator characters and passed to send_file as download_name; paths use generated names.
requirements.verification: Inspect the full quoted requirement against the referenced implementation and rerun the container suite; deployment-specific claims require the recorded proxy/role probes.

requirements.requirement: Verify that file names served (e.g., in HTTP response header fields or email attachments) are encoded or sanitized (e.g., following RFC 6266) to preserve document structure and prevent injection attacks.
requirements.rationale: The served filename is sanitised at upload and encoded at download. _safe_original_name strips path separators and every non-printable character, removes quotes and angle brackets, and truncates to 255 - so a newline cannot forge a log line and a quote cannot break out of the header. Werkzeug's send_file then builds the Content-Disposition itself, emitting RFC 6266 filename* with percent-encoding for anything non-ASCII rather than interpolating the name into the header.
requirements.verification: Re-run tests/test_uploads.py's filename tests; upload a file whose name contains a quote, a newline and a non-ASCII character, and inspect the Content-Disposition on the download.

requirements.requirement: Verify that files obtained from untrusted sources are scanned by antivirus scanners to prevent serving of known malicious content.
requirements.rationale: No antivirus or malware scanning exists. Image re-encoding destroys polyglots and strips metadata, and it is not a substitute: a PDF or a text file is stored exactly as received. The serving controls are real but address a different threat - attachment disposition, a sandbox CSP and nosniff stop a file executing in this origin, and owner-only authorisation means one account's upload is not reachable by another - so what remains is that a malicious document is served back to the owner who uploaded it, unchanged, to open in their own reader. Recorded honestly; no exception is approved, and the absence of a demonstrated cross-account path does not close it.
requirements.verification: Add a scanner in the upload path - ClamAV as a compose service is the usual shape - fail closed when it is unreachable, and add a test that an EICAR test file is refused. Until then the row stays Not met.

requirements.requirement: Verify that application documentation defines how controls such as rate limiting, anti-automation, and adaptive response, are used to defend against attacks such as credential stuffing and password brute force. The documentation must make clear how these controls are configured and prevent malicious account lockout.
requirements.rationale: docs/security/POLICIES.md section 2 tabulates every rate limit with the constant that sets it, states that the adaptive response is account lockout, and states how malicious lockout is prevented: the lock is capped at LOCKOUT_MAX_SECONDS and expires unaided, so a griefer cannot convert a guessing attack into a durable denial of service against the real owner. It also records that the limiter fails closed when its store is unreachable.
requirements.verification: Read POLICIES.md section 2 against validation.py's rate-limit constants and User.lock_duration; confirm each documented limit is the one the decorator applies.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a list of context-specific words is documented in order to prevent their use in passwords. The list could include permutations of organization names, product names, system identifiers, project codenames, department or role names, and similar.
requirements.rationale: validation.CONTEXT_WORDS documents the list - doom, inventory, warehouse, organizer, organiser, storage - and POLICIES.md section 3 explains what it is for and how it differs from the breach corpus: a breach list screens what the world has already guessed, this screens what an attacker who knows what they are looking at would try first. The policy also tells operators to extend it with their organisation and site names, and says why the list is code rather than configuration: a change to it is then reviewed and tested.
requirements.verification: Read POLICIES.md section 3 against validation.CONTEXT_WORDS; re-run TestContextWordScreen.

Nothing about that verification happens on the client.

The share handle is nonetheless generated by secrets.token_urlsafe(16), 128 bits, so the question does not turn on that argument.

requirements.requirement: Verify that when session termination is triggered (such as logout or expiration), the application disallows any further use of the session. For reference tokens or stateful sessions, this means invalidating the session data at the application backend. Applications using self-contained tokens will need a solution such as maintaining a list of terminated tokens, disallowing tokens produced before a per-user date and time or rotating a per-user signing key.

requirements.requirement: Verify that only algorithms on an allowlist can be used to create and verify self-contained tokens, for a given context. This should include ensuring that keys are not overshared (for example, with more than two entities for shared secrets and more than one entity for private keys).
requirements.rationale: POLICIES.md section 6 sets out the policy and the lifecycle: what each key is, how it is created, where it is stored, who rotates it, and what rotation does. Oversharing is bounded by construction - each key is held by exactly the two parties that need it, the application and the store it authenticates to - and secrets are read from mode-0400 files rather than the environment, so they do not appear in docker inspect or in any child process's environ, a property make verify-secrets checks rather than assumes. What remains an operator obligation is named as one: custody of the host directory, the rotation schedule and destruction of superseded copies.
requirements.verification: Read POLICIES.md section 6 against config._read_secret and the compose secret mounts; run make verify-secrets against a live stack.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a cryptographic inventory is performed, maintained, regularly updated, and includes all cryptographic keys, algorithms, and certificates used by the application. It must also document where keys can and cannot be used in the system, and the types of data that can and cannot be protected using the keys.
requirements.rationale: POLICIES.md section 16 is the inventory: every key, its algorithm and size, where it may be used and where it must not, plus the certificates and the agility position. It names the boundaries the requirement asks for explicitly - SECRET_KEY is never an encryption key, attachment digests are content addresses and not an integrity guarantee against an attacker with database write access, audit row hashes are tamper evidence and not proof, and TLS certificates are not used for internal service authentication because internal traffic is unencrypted.
requirements.verification: Read POLICIES.md section 16 against the code it names; confirm each listed key appears only where the table permits.

requirements.requirement: Verify that industry-validated implementations (including libraries and hardware-accelerated implementations) are used for cryptographic operations.
requirements.rationale: Everything cryptographic comes from hashlib, hmac and secrets - which is OpenSSL - or from argon2-cffi, which is the Argon2 reference implementation. The one piece of arithmetic written here rather than imported is the TOTP step function, and it is thirty lines of those same standard-library primitives pinned to the RFC 4226 and RFC 6238 published vectors; the primitives it composes are still the validated ones.
requirements.verification: Re-run tests/test_totp.py, which runs every published vector; confirm no third-party crypto library other than argon2-cffi is in the lockfile.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application is designed with crypto agility such that random number, authenticated encryption, MAC, or hashing algorithms, key lengths, rounds, ciphers and modes can be reconfigured, upgraded, or swapped at any time, to protect against cryptographic breaks. Similarly, it must also be possible to replace keys and passwords and re-encrypt data. This will allow for seamless upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), once high-assurance implementations of approved PQC schemes or standards are widely available.
requirements.rationale: Every algorithm choice is one named constant or one class attribute in one module - password parameters in security/passwords.py, the signing digest in security/sessions.py, the TOTP construction in security/totp.py - so swapping one is an edit in a single place rather than a search. Password hashes carry their own parameters, so raising the cost re-hashes each account silently at its owner's next sign-in; raising the signing digest changes the salt with it, which invalidates issued cookies rather than leaving them verifiable under the weaker algorithm. There is no encrypted data at rest, so there is nothing to re-encrypt.
requirements.verification: Read POLICIES.md section 16's agility paragraph; change the Argon2 parameters and confirm needs_rehash upgrades an account at its next sign-in.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all cryptographic primitives utilize a minimum of 128-bits of security based on the algorithm, key size, and configuration. For example, a 256-bit ECC key provides roughly 128 bits of security where RSA requires a 3072-bit key to achieve 128 bits of security.
requirements.rationale: Every primitive is at or above 128 bits of security: HMAC-SHA256 with a 256-bit key for the session cookie and the CSRF serializer, SHA-256 for content addressing and the audit chain, Argon2id with a 256-bit output and a 128-bit salt for passwords, 256-bit share tokens, 128-bit share handles, and TLS suites offering 128-bit security or better. The TOTP secret is 160 bits as RFC 4226 specifies; its HMAC-SHA1 construction is the documented exception in section 6, and a 30-second six-digit code is bounded by rate limiting and single use rather than by hash strength.
requirements.verification: Read POLICIES.md section 16's size column against the generators in the code; enumerate the TLS suites the live edge offers.

requirements.requirement: Verify that insecure block modes (e.g., ECB) and weak padding schemes (e.g., PKCS#1 v1.5) are not used.
requirements.rationale: The application performs no symmetric encryption, so there is no block mode or padding scheme to choose badly: an AST walk over the package finds no cipher use, and the only cryptographic primitives are Argon2id, HMAC-SHA256 and SHA-256. The one encrypted channel is TLS at the edge, where Caddy offers only AEAD cipher suites - ECDHE with AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 - and ECB and PKCS#1 v1.5 are not among them.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_no_withdrawn_hash_is_reachable_from_the_package; enumerate the offered suites against the running edge and confirm all are AEAD.

requirements.requirement: Verify that only approved ciphers and modes such as AES with GCM are used.

requirements.verification: Re-run the TLS cases in evidence/proxy-edge-headers.txt; enumerate offered suites and confirm no CBC or RC4 suite is present.

Where integrity does matter it is provided directly rather than as a property of encryption: the session cookie is MACed with HMAC-SHA256, and the audit log is a SHA-256 hash chain. The one encrypted channel is TLS, whose suites are AEAD-only and therefore authenticated by construction.

requirements.requirement: Verify that only approved hash functions are used for general cryptographic use cases, including digital signatures, HMAC, KDF, and random bit generation. Disallowed hash functions, such as MD5, must not be used for any cryptographic purpose.
requirements.rationale: Argon2id for passwords and share PINs, HMAC-SHA256 for the session cookie, the CSRF serializer and the share PIN approval, SHA-256 for content addressing and the audit hash chain, and os.urandom by way of the secrets module for random bit generation. No MD5, SHA-1 or SHA-224 is reachable from the package, and the test that asserts it walks the AST rather than grepping, so the paragraph in security/sessions.py that explains why SHA-1 is not used does not itself trip the check.

requirements.requirement: Verify that passwords are stored using an approved, computationally intensive, key derivation function (also known as a "password hashing function"), with parameter settings configured based on current guidance. The settings should balance security and performance to make brute-force attacks sufficiently challenging for the required level of security.
requirements.rationale: Argon2id at t=3, 64 MiB and p=4, which exceeds the OWASP floor of 19 MiB and t=2. Memory cost is the load-bearing figure rather than iterations: at 64 MiB per hash an attacker needs 64 GiB to run a thousand guesses in parallel, which is what makes large-scale offline cracking expensive rather than merely slow. The same figure is a capacity constraint on this side, which is why gunicorn concurrency is pinned in compose and PASSWORD_MAX caps the input - the balance the requirement asks for is made explicitly rather than inherited from a default.
requirements.verification: Read the parameter block in security/passwords.py and D-02; time a verification and confirm it is in the expected range for these settings.

No hash shorter than 256 bits is used where collision resistance is required - the 160-bit TOTP construction needs neither collision nor second-preimage resistance, only MAC unforgeability over a 30-second window.

The requirement's note about UUIDs is respected rather than tripped over - row identifiers are UUID4 and are used as identifiers, never as credentials; the one place a UUID travels in a cookie it is inside a MACed session and confers nothing on its own.

Caddy's default minimum was already 1.2; the Caddyfile now states the policy explicitly so a future default cannot lower it silently and so the setting is reviewable without knowing which Caddy version shipped which default. The probe confirms a TLS 1.1 handshake is refused and a TLS 1.3 one completes.

requirements.requirement: Verify that external facing services use publicly trusted TLS certificates.
requirements.rationale: Not met literally, and the reason is the deployment rather than a missing capability. The reviewed deployment serves DOOM_DOMAIN=localhost, for which no public CA can issue, so Caddy presents its own internal CA; the compensating control is that the CA reaches the devices that need it out of band through `make trust-cert` rather than being clicked through, on a private network with no public name. Three routes to a publicly trusted certificate are supported and documented in caddy/conf.d/README.md, none of which needs a custom image: an existing reverse proxy terminating TLS in front of this stack, a certificate this deployment did not issue mounted and named with `tls`, or Caddy's own ACME, which engages automatically for any publicly resolvable DOOM_DOMAIN. `make verify-cert` guards the second, where nothing renews the file automatically. Recorded as a finding, not accepted: no exception is approved, and no such deployment has been assessed.
requirements.verification: On the first non-local deployment, confirm the served chain terminates in a publicly trusted root from a client with no custom CA installed, and re-run the release gate with --deployment non-local. Where the certificate comes from a file, `make verify-cert` must also pass - it compares the file on disk against what is actually being served.

requirements.requirement: Verify that an encrypted protocol such as TLS is used for all inbound and outbound connections to and from the application, including monitoring systems, management tools, remote access and SSH, middleware, databases, mainframes, partner systems, or external APIs. The server must not fall back to insecure or unencrypted protocols.
requirements.rationale: Not met literally. Caddy reaches the application over plaintext HTTP, and the application reaches PostgreSQL and Redis over plaintext, on Docker networks that carry nothing else. What has changed since this was assessed is the boundary rather than the encryption: those networks are now all internal, the application container has no route off the host at all, and the only process that touches the outside is Caddy, which terminates TLS. So the plaintext exists inside a boundary that is narrower than it was, and there is no inbound or outbound connection crossing the host unencrypted. That is a mitigation, not the control - an attacker with the Docker host, or a second workload on it, reads this traffic. Recorded as a finding; no exception is approved.
requirements.verification: Issue internal certificates and enable TLS on the Postgres and Redis listeners with the client configured to verify them; put the application behind TLS from Caddy. Until then, confirm no service other than caddy is on the edge network and no port other than Caddy's is published.

Authentication must use individual service accounts, short-term tokens, or certificate-based authentication and not unchanging credentials such as passwords, API keys, or shared accounts with privileged access.

It asks for individual service accounts with short-term tokens or certificate-based authentication, and unchanging credentials are named as the thing not to use. Recorded as Not met rather than compensated, because the mitigations here reduce exposure of the credential without changing its nature.

This depends on 12.3.1 being closed first: certificate authentication needs a TLS channel to present a certificate on.

requirements.rationale: Two database roles, and the application never gets the powerful one. The runtime connects as a restricted role that cannot ALTER or DROP and, for audit_log, has had UPDATE and DELETE revoked - so the application cannot rewrite its own history even if it is compromised. Migrations use a separate admin DSN supplied only by make upgrade to a one-off container. The privilege rules are applied by an idempotent `flask db-grants` rather than living in a migration, so they are not conditional on a schema revision having run, and make verify-db-roles asserts the outcome in CI.

requirements.rationale: No default credential exists anywhere in the deployment. make init generates every secret with openssl rand; config.py refuses to start when a required value is missing or still holds a placeholder, and the placeholder list includes the obvious ones; the database role name is configurable and its password is generated; and the application's own demo account now generates its password rather than publishing one. A crash loop on a misconfigured boot is deliberate - a deployment that starts anyway with a guessable secret is worse than one that refuses.

requirements.requirement: Verify that an allowlist is used to define the external resources or systems with which the application is permitted to communicate (e.g., for outbound requests, data loads, or file access). This allowlist can be implemented at the application layer, web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers.
requirements.rationale: Expressed as a deny-all, which is the only version of an allowlist that cannot be incomplete. The application container sits on two internal-only Docker networks and has no route off the host: it can reach the database and the cache, Caddy can reach it, and that is the entire set of destinations that exist. At the application layer there is additionally an allowlist of barcode providers in code, but that is now the inner of two layers rather than the only one. Enabling outbound access means adding the edge network back to the service in docker-compose.yml, which is a reviewable change rather than a default.
requirements.verification: Inspect the networks block in docker-compose.yml; from inside a running web container, attempt an outbound connection and confirm it fails.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the web or application server is configured with an allowlist of resources or systems to which the server can send requests or load data or files from.
requirements.rationale: Same control as 13.2.4, read from the server's side: the web container has no egress route, so there is no destination it can send a request to or load a file from beyond the two services on its internal networks. This is the layer the requirement asks for - configured at the infrastructure rather than in the application - and it is what makes an SSRF in the lookup path reach nothing, which matters because the DNS-rebinding defect in that path is not closed.
requirements.verification: Inspect docker-compose.yml; attempt an outbound connection from inside the running web container and confirm it is refused at the network layer rather than by application validation.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a secrets management solution, such as a key vault, is used to securely create, store, control access to, and destroy backend secrets. These could include passwords, key material, integrations with databases and third-party systems, keys and seeds for time-based tokens, other internal secrets, and API keys. Secrets must not be included in application source code or included in build artifacts. For an L3 application, this must involve a hardware-backed solution such as an HSM.
requirements.rationale: There is no key vault. Secrets are generated by make init, held in a restricted host directory, mounted read-only into the containers and read from files rather than the environment - which covers storage and access control, and make verify-secrets proves the environment half rather than asserting it. What a vault would add is managed creation, rotation and destruction with an audit trail, and those remain operator tasks with no verified lifecycle evidence. The mount point is the seam where a vault would attach. L3's hardware-backed requirement is not met and is not claimed. Recorded as a finding; no exception is approved.
requirements.verification: Introduce a secrets manager that issues and rotates these credentials, and record rotation and destruction evidence. Until then, run make verify-secrets and confirm the host directory's permissions.

requirements.requirement: Verify that access to secret assets adheres to the principle of least privilege.
requirements.rationale: Each secret is readable by exactly the service that needs it and by nothing else: compose mounts each file into the one container that uses it, mode 0400, read-only, and the application reads it once at startup rather than holding it in an environment every child process would inherit. make verify-secrets checks the negative directly - that no secret value appears in docker inspect output or in any process environment inside the container - which is the property that was previously assumed and turned out to be false when a shell entrypoint was exporting a finished DSN.
requirements.verification: Run make verify-secrets against a live stack; inspect the mount modes in docker-compose.yml.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application is deployed either without any source control metadata, including the .git or .svn folders, or in a way that these folders are inaccessible both externally and to the application itself.
requirements.rationale: The build context is ./app, and .git lives at the repository root, so version-control metadata is not in the context at all. The image is then built from an explicit COPY allowlist - doom, migrations and wsgi.py - rather than a COPY of the context, so nothing arrives by accident, and .dockerignore excludes VCS and editor debris as a second line. The uploads volume, the only writable path, contains no repository data.
requirements.verification: Inspect the COPY lines in app/Dockerfile; run `docker run --rm <image> ls -a /srv/doom` and confirm no .git; confirm the build context root contains no VCS directory.

requirements.requirement: Verify that debug modes are disabled for all components in production environments to prevent exposure of debugging features and information leakage.
requirements.rationale: Debug is not a toggle in this application. DEBUG and TESTING are False on the base configuration, the factory raises if DEBUG is set, and Config.verify_runtime raises when FLASK_DEBUG or DEBUG is present in the environment - checked separately because an environment variable would otherwise switch on the interactive debugger without touching the config class. The debugger is a remote code execution console, so the response is a refusal to boot rather than a warning. Caddy's admin API is off, and the runtime image ships no test runner.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_debug_is_not_a_toggle, which sets each variable and asserts the refusal; start the stack with FLASK_DEBUG=1 and confirm it will not boot.

requirements.requirement: Verify that web servers do not expose directory listings to clients unless explicitly intended.
requirements.rationale: Neither layer can list a directory. Caddy has no file_server directive at all - the uploads volume is deliberately not mounted there, because a file_server over it would bypass every ownership check in the application - and Flask's static handler serves named files without an index. A test requests several directory paths and confirms each answers 404 or 405 rather than a listing.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_no_route_lists_a_directory; request a directory path against the live edge.

requirements.requirement: Verify that using the HTTP TRACE method is not supported in production environments, to avoid potential information leakage.
requirements.rationale: TRACE is not routed and not implemented: Werkzeug's router answers 405 for it on every path, and Caddy does not add one. A test issues TRACE against the application and asserts it is refused rather than echoed.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_trace_is_not_answered; issue TRACE against the live edge.

requirements.requirement: Verify that documentation (such as for internal APIs) and monitoring endpoints are not exposed unless explicitly intended.
requirements.rationale: There is no API documentation endpoint, no schema endpoint, no metrics endpoint and no debug console - a test asserts none of the usual paths is registered. requirements.requirement: Verify that all sensitive data created and processed by the application has been identified and classified into protection levels. This includes data that is only encoded and therefore easily decoded, such as Base64 strings or the plaintext payload inside a JWT. Protection levels need to take into account any data protection and privacy regulations and standards which the application is required to comply with.
requirements.rationale: POLICIES.md section 11 classifies everything the application creates or processes into six protection levels - secret, credential, personal, inventory, shared-by-choice and public - and says what falls in each. It addresses the requirement's specific point about merely-encoded data: a share token is random rather than derived so there is nothing in it to decode, and the audit chain's row hashes are integrity values published on purpose rather than concealed ones. The regulatory scope is stated: a single-tenant self-hosted inventory, no payment or health data, operator as controller where GDPR applies.
requirements.verification: Read POLICIES.md section 11 against the model columns; confirm every column in models.py falls into one of the six levels.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all sensitive data protection levels have a documented set of protection requirements. This must include (but not be limited to) requirements related to general encryption, integrity verification, retention, how the data is to be logged, access controls around sensitive data in logs, database-level encryption, privacy and privacy-enhancing technologies to be used, and other confidentiality requirements.
requirements.rationale: Each of the six levels in POLICIES.md section 11 carries its own handling requirements rather than a shared paragraph: how it is stored, whether it may be logged and in what form, what response headers apply, whether it may appear in a URL, and what access control governs it. Retention is stated per level, including the deliberate asymmetry that audit rows are never deleted by the application - including by the account they describe, because a history a user can edit is not a history. Encryption at rest is named as absent rather than implied.
requirements.verification: Read POLICIES.md section 11's handling column against the logging redaction lists, the header hook and the storage code.

requirements.requirement: Verify that sensitive data is only sent to the server in the HTTP message body or header fields, and that the URL and query string do not contain sensitive information, such as an API key or session token.
requirements.rationale: The one credential this application puts in front of an unauthenticated visitor no longer travels in a URL. A label encodes https://host/t/#<code>; a fragment is never transmitted, so scanning one sends the server GET /t/ and nothing more. The unlock page moves the code into a POST body, the server files it in the visitor's signed session and redirects to /t/v/<handle>, where the handle names an entry in that cookie and addresses nothing without it. Nothing else sensitive is ever placed in a URL or query string: identifiers in paths are UUIDs that still require a session.
requirements.verification: Re-run TestShareCodeNeverInAURL, which checks the generated label URL, the landing request, the redirect target, a second client's attempt on the same handle, the cap on held codes and handle reuse.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application prevents sensitive data from being cached in server components, such as load balancers and application caches, or ensures that the data is securely purged after use.
requirements.rationale: Nothing sensitive is cached in a server component, because there is no server-side cache to hold it: no application cache, no CDN, no reverse-proxy response cache - Caddy is configured to proxy, not to cache. Redis holds rate-limit counters keyed by IP and route, and no user data at all. Every authenticated response additionally carries Cache-Control: no-store with Vary: Cookie, so an intermediary that is added later cannot begin caching them silently.
requirements.verification: Inspect caddy/Caddyfile for a cache directive; inspect what is written to Redis; re-run the anti-caching tests in tests/test_headers.py.

requirements.requirement: Verify that defined sensitive data is not sent to untrusted parties (e.g., user trackers) to prevent unwanted collection of data outside of the application's control.
requirements.rationale: No data is sent to any third party, because there is no third party: no analytics, no trackers, no error-reporting service, no CDN, no webfont, no third-party script or stylesheet. The CSP states it - connect-src 'self', script-src 'self', style-src 'self', form-action 'self' - and the deny-all network position enforces it, since the application container has no route off the host at all. Referrer-Policy: same-origin additionally means a URL is not disclosed to a site a user clicks through to.

requirements.requirement: Verify that controls around sensitive data related to encryption, integrity verification, retention, how the data is to be logged, access controls around sensitive data in logs, privacy and privacy-enhancing technologies, are implemented as defined in the documentation for the specific data's protection level.
requirements.rationale: The controls POLICIES.md section 11 assigns per level are implemented: secrets are Argon2id hashed and never logged, credentials are redacted from logs by key, by path and by shape and kept out of URLs, personal and inventory data are owner-scoped and carry no-store, shared views carry only the serializer's fields with noindex and rate limits, and audit rows are append-only at the database-role level. The three redaction mechanisms cover the three shapes a secret arrives in - a structured field, a URL path, and free text in a message or a traceback.

requirements.requirement: Verify that authenticated data is cleared from client storage, such as the browser DOM, after the client or session is terminated. The 'Clear-Site-Data' HTTP response header field may be able to help with this but the client-side should also be able to clear up if the server connection is not available when the session is terminated.
requirements.rationale: Sign-out sends Clear-Site-Data for cache, cookies and storage, so the browser drops what it holds for this origin rather than only the cookie; authenticated pages are already Cache-Control: no-store with Vary: Cookie, so little is left to clear and nothing is in an intermediary cache. executionContexts is deliberately not requested - browsers disagree about whether it takes effect before or after the redirect completes, which has produced reload loops - and the volatile DOM goes with the navigation that follows. Nothing authenticated is written to localStorage or sessionStorage, so there is no client-side state to clean up when the server is unreachable.
requirements.verification: Re-run TestClearSiteDataOnLogout; grep the scripts for localStorage and sessionStorage; sign out over HTTPS and confirm the header is honoured.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application sets sufficient anti-caching HTTP response header fields (i.e., Cache-Control: no-store) so that sensitive data is not cached in browsers.
requirements.rationale: Cache-Control: no-store on every authenticated response, with Pragma: no-cache for HTTP/1.0 caches and Vary: Cookie so a shared cache cannot serve one user's page to another. It is deliberately no-store rather than private with a max-age, including for image thumbnails: the data is a map to physical property, so a page sitting in the cache of a shared machine after somebody walks away is a real disclosure path. Static assets are exempt because they contain no user data.
requirements.verification: Re-run tests/test_headers.py's caching tests and test_authenticated_pages_are_never_stored; inspect the header on a live authenticated response.

requirements.requirement: Verify that data stored in browser storage (such as localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, or cookies) does not contain sensitive data, with the exception of session tokens.
requirements.rationale: Nothing is written to browser storage at all. There is no localStorage, sessionStorage or IndexedDB use anywhere in the four scripts - they render text into the DOM and read a camera, and keep no state between page loads. The session token lives in an HttpOnly cookie, which is the exception the requirement explicitly permits, and appears nowhere a script could read it.
requirements.verification: Grep app/doom/static/js for localStorage, sessionStorage and indexedDB; load each page and inspect browser storage after signing in.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application has implemented defenses against loss of availability due to functionality which is time-consuming or resource-demanding, based on the documented security decisions and strategies for this.
requirements.rationale: Each bound in POLICIES.md section 14 is enforced where it is documented: PASSWORD_MAX caps hashing input and the rate limits and lockout cap attempts; MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS is checked before decoding rather than after, which is the difference between refusing a decompression bomb and decoding one; the export is owner-scoped and rate limited. Worker concurrency times the Argon2id memory cost is pinned in compose to fit the container's memory limit, so the expensive path cannot exhaust the host. Authenticated views render the owner's own rows, where the subset question does not arise, and the JSON endpoints return fixed literal keys.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application has countermeasures to protect against mass assignment attacks by limiting allowed fields per controller and action, e.g., it is not possible to insert or update a field value when it was not intended to be part of that action.
requirements.rationale: No view binds a request to a model. Every assignment is field by field from a validated form and nothing uses **request.form, which is why a posted is_active, session_version, password_hash, id or totp_secret has nothing to bind to - a test submits all five to the profile form and confirms none of them moves. The forms themselves are the allowlist, and they are per action rather than per model: the profile form carries three fields and the password form carries different ones, so a field that is legitimate in one action cannot be smuggled into another.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all proxying and middleware components transfer the user's original IP address correctly using trusted data fields that cannot be manipulated by the end user, and the application and web server use this correct value for logging and security decisions such as rate limiting, taking into account that even the original IP address may not be reliable due to dynamic IPs, VPNs, or corporate firewalls.
requirements.rationale: Caddy pins X-Forwarded-For to {client_ip} rather than appending to what arrived, and ProxyFix trusts exactly one hop, so the address the application logs and rate-limits on is the one the proxy wrote. With no trusted proxy declared that is the direct peer and a forged chain is ignored, which a test drives through the configured middleware; when a homelab puts its own Traefik or Caddy in front and declares it trusted, the real client survives the extra hop instead of collapsing every visitor into one rate-limit bucket. The requirement's caveat is respected in the design rather than ignored: the address is used for rate limiting and the audit trail, never as an authorization input, precisely because a shared NAT or a VPN makes it an unreliable identity.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_a_client_cannot_forge_the_address_used_for_rate_limiting; send a forged chain through the live edge and confirm the logged address is the peer's.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application explicitly ensures that variables are of the correct type and performs strict equality and comparator operations. This is to avoid type juggling or type confusion vulnerabilities caused by the application code making an assumption about a variable type.
requirements.rationale: Python has no type juggling of the kind this requirement is written against - there is no == coercion between a string and an integer, and no loose comparison operator to reach for. Where a value does need to become a type it is converted explicitly and a failure is a miss rather than an exception: a path parameter is parsed to a UUID and returns 404 if it will not parse, form fields are coerced by their field type, and the session's own values are checked with isinstance before use. Secret comparisons use hmac.compare_digest rather than ==.
requirements.verification: Re-run tests/test_access_control.py with malformed identifiers; submit a non-numeric quantity and confirm a form error rather than a 500.

requirements.requirement: Verify that JavaScript code is written in a way that prevents prototype pollution, for example, by using Set() or Map() instead of object literals.
requirements.rationale: There are no object literals used as maps and no merge or deep-assign of untrusted data in any of the four scripts - the pattern prototype pollution needs. They read a camera, write textContent, and in one case read a URL fragment, validate it against a fixed pattern and put it in a form field. No script parses JSON from a server response into an object whose keys then index anything.

requirements.rationale: Werkzeug distinguishes sources rather than merging them - request.form, request.args and request.cookies are separate MultiDicts, and a form reads the one it is given - so a value cannot move between the query string and the body to change which one wins. A repeated key returns its first value, deterministically. A test posts a duplicated field with a third value in the query string and asserts the first body value is what lands.

It records that nothing is written to a file inside any container - the filesystem is read-only apart from the uploads volume and a tmpfs - and that nothing is broadcast anywhere else, which is the open gap at 16.4.3 rather than an omission from the inventory. Correlation ids are documented as the mechanism that ties a user's report to exact lines without showing them a traceback.
