requirements.rationale: Every log line carries when (ISO-8601 with an explicit UTC offset), where (logger name, request method and scrubbed path), who (the acting account on audit rows, the source address on request lines) and what (the event name and its structured fields), plus a correlation id that ties the lines of one request together. Audit rows carry the same metadata in columns, with the actor's username denormalised onto the row so a later rename does not rewrite history.

requirements.requirement: Verify that time sources for all logging components are synchronized, and that timestamps in security event metadata use UTC or include an explicit time zone offset. UTC is recommended to ensure consistency across distributed systems and to prevent confusion during daylight saving time transitions.
requirements.rationale: The application's half is met and testable: every timestamp is UTC with an explicit offset, in the log formatter and in the database, so there is no daylight-saving ambiguity to resolve. The half that is not met is that all four containers take their clock from the host kernel, so their timestamps agree with each other by construction but their accuracy is the host's - and no evidence exists that the host runs NTP. That is an operator obligation no code in this repository can discharge, and it is recorded rather than assumed. Container-to-container consistency is the compensating property; absolute accuracy is not established.
requirements.verification: Confirm the host runs a time synchronisation service and record its status as operator evidence. The application-side property can be re-checked by inspecting any log line's offset.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application only stores or broadcasts logs to the files and services that are documented in the log inventory.
requirements.rationale: The destinations in POLICIES.md section 12 are the only ones: stdout for every container, and the audit_log table. Nothing writes to a file inside a container - the application's filesystem is read-only apart from the uploads volume and a 64 MB tmpfs, so it could not - and no log shipper, syslog forwarder or third-party sink is configured. The inventory and the reality therefore agree by construction rather than by review.

requirements.rationale: One line of JSON per event, from every layer that the application controls: the application logger, gunicorn's access log through a custom formatter, and Caddy's own JSON output. Field names are shared across them - timestamp, level, method, path, ip, correlation_id - so a processor can correlate a request across the edge and the application without a per-source parser, which is what the requirement's preference for a common format is for.

requirements.requirement: Verify that when logging sensitive data, the application enforces logging based on the data's protection level. For example, it may not be allowed to log certain data, such as credentials or payment details. Other data, such as session tokens, may only be logged by being hashed or masked, either in full or partially.
requirements.rationale: Three mechanisms, because a secret arrives in three shapes and a key-based redaction covers only one. Structured fields are redacted by key name; request paths and Referer URLs are scrubbed after percent-decoding, so /t/<code> and /%74/<code> are both reduced; and free-text messages and exception tracebacks are now scrubbed for share-code-shaped values and for key=value pairs whose key is sensitive - the gap that made this Partial, since a message has no keys and a library's exception text is not ours to choose. A test confirms an ordinary message survives intact, because a log nobody can read is replaced by one nobody redacts.

requirements.rationale: A refused object access writes an access_denied row before the 404 that follows it, and the commit is load-bearing rather than incidental: every caller aborts immediately afterwards, so without an explicit commit the row would be discarded with the rolled-back session and enumeration would be invisible. A malformed identifier is deliberately not audited - garbage in a path is a broken link, and recording it would hand any user a table to flood.

Security control failures are logged specifically rather than swallowed: a failed audit write, a failed session revocation, an unreadable password hash in the database, a libmagic failure, and a failed user lookup each log at error or exception level with context. requirements.requirement: Verify that all logging components appropriately encode data to prevent log injection.
requirements.rationale: Every log line is JSON produced by json.dumps, which escapes newlines, quotes and control characters as it serialises - so a value cannot terminate a line and forge the next one, which is what log injection is. That covers the structured fields and the message alike. Upstream of it, a filename is stripped of newlines, tabs and quotes at upload for the same reason, so the value is already inert before it reaches a formatter.

requirements.requirement: Verify that logs are protected from unauthorized access and cannot be modified.
requirements.rationale: The application cannot rewrite its own history: UPDATE and DELETE on audit_log are revoked from the restricted role the runtime uses, so a compromise of the application does not become a compromise of the record, and the hash chain makes any out-of-band modification evident. Those are the two properties that can be established from inside this repository. What cannot is protection of the container's stdout stream on the host, its retention, and access control over it - all of which belong to the operator and have no evidence. Recorded as a finding rather than claimed.
requirements.verification: Run make verify-db-roles and attempt an UPDATE on audit_log as the application role; for the rest, record the host's log store permissions and retention as operator evidence.

requirements.requirement: Verify that logs are securely transmitted to a logically separate system for analysis, detection, alerting, and escalation. The aim is to ensure that if the application is breached, the logs are not compromised.
requirements.rationale: Logs stay on the host that produces them. There is no shipper, no separate analysis system, no alerting and no escalation path, so the property this requirement exists for - that a breach of the application does not also compromise the record of it - does not hold for the stdout stream. The append-only database table and its hash chain are a partial answer for the audit trail specifically and are already credited at 16.4.2; they are not log shipping, and treating them as such would be the kind of substitution this assessment is written to avoid. Recorded honestly; no exception is approved.
requirements.verification: Configure a log driver or sidecar shipping to a separate system, with alerting on the authentication and access-denial events, and record delivery evidence. This is a deployment obligation and is listed in the hosted-readiness assessment.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a generic message is returned to the consumer when an unexpected or security-sensitive error occurs, ensuring no exposure of sensitive internal system data such as stack traces, queries, secret keys, and tokens.
requirements.rationale: The user gets a plain sentence and a twelve-character correlation id; the server gets the type, the traceback and the request. Messages are generic by design - 'no such user' versus 'wrong password', or 'item not found' versus 'forbidden', are both small oracles - and there is a template-free fallback page for the case where template rendering is itself what failed, so an error handler that raises cannot fall through to the framework's default traceback page. A test asserts a 500 carries no traceback, no exception type, no file path, no query fragment and no key.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_an_unexpected_error_returns_a_correlation_id_and_nothing_else; raise inside a view and inspect the response body.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application continues to operate securely when external resource access fails, for example, by using patterns such as circuit breakers or graceful degradation.
requirements.rationale: There is one external dependency, the optional barcode lookup, and its failure degrades rather than breaks: the caller returns a fixed 'unavailable' message with no provider detail, records an audit row, and the rest of the page continues to work - a test confirms the response carries no internal address and that the application remains usable afterwards. The internal dependencies fail the other way on purpose: the rate limiter refuses requests when its store is unreachable rather than lifting the limits, because for a security control graceful degradation means failing closed.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_an_external_lookup_failure_degrades_rather_than_breaks; stop Redis and confirm requests are refused rather than allowed through unlimited.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application fails gracefully and securely, including when an exception occurs, preventing fail-open conditions such as processing a transaction despite errors resulting from validation logic.
requirements.rationale: A refused form writes nothing - the write is inside the validated branch, not after it, so there is no path where validation fails and the transaction proceeds; a test asserts the row count is unchanged after a rejected submission. The same shape holds elsewhere: a failed PIN returns 401 without rendering the content, a failed re-authentication re-renders the page without applying any field, and an exception mid-request is rolled back by the context teardown. Where a control cannot do its job it fails closed: the limiter refuses, the configuration refuses to boot, and the user loader returns None rather than a partially validated user.
requirements.verification: Re-run test_validation_failure_does_not_fall_through_to_the_write and TestSequentialFlows; force an exception mid-request and confirm no partial row survives.
